title: AI-Augmented Engineering: Working with Coding Agents
tagline: The daily craft of working with an AI coding agent: brief it well, drive the session, and review what it made as if a stranger wrote it.
description: A coding agent is a fast, literal junior engineer with no memory of yesterday and no idea what you did not tell it. This course teaches the craft inside a session: a standing brief the agent reads every time, skills for repeatable work, plans before builds, guardrails in code, and a review posture that catches the specific ways agents fail. You practice on the same tiny bookshop app as Spec-Driven Development for Dummies, with the coding agent Quill, and Eve, the built-in tutor, is one highlight away.
audience: Engineers who use, or are about to use, a terminal coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor's agent, Copilot's agent mode, and the like) for real work. You can read TypeScript, run tests, and review a pull request. No AI background is assumed.

verbs.name: Brief
verbs.question: What does the agent need to know before it starts, and where does that knowledge live?

verbs.name: Drive
verbs.question: How do you run a session so the agent does the right work, and how do you stop it doing the wrong work?

verbs.name: Review
verbs.question: How do you check what it made, and how do you turn each mistake into a rule?

runningExample.title: Bramble Books, Shelf, and Quill
runningExample.summary: The same world as Spec-Driven Development for Dummies. Bramble Books is a small bookshop chain; Shelf is its TypeScript web app (inventory, orders, gift cards, customer emails); Quill is the coding agent, running on Claude Code. Omar, the engineer, learns the craft; Jun, the senior engineer, reviews his pull requests. Three change requests recur: a low-stock badge, an async/await refactor, and a nightly sales email.

tutorNotes: Prefer the course's running example, shared with Spec-Driven Development for Dummies: Bramble Books, a small bookshop chain; Shelf, its TypeScript web app (src/orders, src/giftcards, src/inventory, src/email, tests/ with Vitest, migrations/, make test); and Quill, the coding agent, which runs on Claude Code. The cast: Omar (the engineer, the learner), Jun (the senior engineer who reviews Omar's PRs and pairs with him), Nadia (product owner), and Priya (policy owner for payments and customer data). The three recurring change requests: CR-110 (a low-stock badge on the inventory list, the ideal first agent task), CR-111 (move the orders module from callbacks to async/await, a large refactor that needs a plan, splitting, and restarts), CR-112 (a nightly job that emails store managers a sales summary, which touches email and scheduling and produced the 1,400-line PR Jun reviewed). The three verbs: Brief (L0-L2), Drive (L3-L4), Review (L5-B1). The one-liner: brief like a lead, drive like a pair, review like a stranger. The six agent failures from L5: scope creep, hollow tests, weakened checks, hallucinated APIs, silent config changes, behavior changes hidden in refactors. The finding-to-rule ladder: a brief line (advisory), a hook (enforced), a test (enforced and proves behavior). Agent configuration uses Claude Code shapes only: CLAUDE.md (project), ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user), CLAUDE.local.md (personal), @file imports, .claude/settings.json with permissions allow/ask/deny and PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks (exit 0 allows, exit 2 blocks, JSON permissionDecision allow/deny/ask), .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md with name and description frontmatter and $ARGUMENTS, .claude/agents/<name>.md subagents, plan mode, /clear, /compact, git worktrees. Do not invent other flags or commands; if asked about a feature outside these, say the course does not cover it and suggest the official documentation. For the lifecycle around a session (specs, gates, evidence) point to Spec-Driven Development for Dummies; for evals point to Building and Evaluating AI Agents.
credits: Written as the day-to-day companion to Spec-Driven Development for Dummies. Agent configuration examples follow Claude Code's documented shapes for memory files, settings, hooks, skills, and subagents. All lesson text, examples, quizzes, the glossary, and the Bramble Books scenes were written for this course.
